notes.meaning: The Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, ended at sunset on Saturday. Three women who had stayed close to Jesus bought spices to honor His body. Nicodemus had already used spices, but these women still wanted to show their own love. They came to care for a dead body, which shows they did not expect Him to rise.

The women probably set out while it was still dark. The sun was coming up by the time they reached the tomb. It was Sunday, the first day of the week. Jesus had lain in the grave part of Friday, all of Saturday, and part of Sunday, so He rose on the third day, just as He said.

On the way, the women kept asking each other who would move the heavy stone. Their love had carried them out without a plan, and God did not blame them for it. They did not even know soldiers were guarding the tomb. Their worry shows they had no hope of finding Jesus alive.

When they looked up, the huge stone was already rolled back. Matthew tells us an angel moved it. It was not moved to let Jesus out, but to let the witnesses in to see the tomb was empty. People who seek Christ with a whole heart often find their problems taken away before they arrive.

Inside the tomb sat a young man in a white robe. Matthew calls him an angel of the Lord, and the white robe marks him as coming from heaven. The women were alarmed. Often the very thing that should comfort us scares us at first, because we do not understand it.

The angel calms them with the best news ever told: Jesus, who was really crucified and dead, is risen. He still calls Him "the Nazarene" and "crucified," names once used in scorn, because His glory now wipes away the shame of the cross. The women can see the empty place for themselves. His rising shows that His payment for our sins was accepted by God.

The women are sent to tell the disciples, and Peter by name. Peter had denied Jesus three times, and he might have thought the good news was not for him. Naming him was a sign of Jesus' forgiveness and love. Jesus would meet them in Galilee, just as He had promised, because He keeps His word.

The women ran from the tomb, shaking and amazed. They spoke to no one they met on the way, perhaps fearing the news was too good to be true. They did report to the disciples later, as Luke shows. Fear can keep us from serving Christ when our faith and joy are weak.

The risen Jesus showed Himself first to Mary Magdalene. Jesus had once freed her from seven demons. She had been forgiven much and loved much, and she was given the honor of seeing Him first. John 20 tells this meeting in full.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The two oldest Greek manuscripts of Mark stop at verse 8, and other copies end in different ways. Many scholars think Mark's first ending was lost and that verses 9-20 were added later as a summary of the other Gospels. Some say no teaching should rest on these verses alone.

notes.meaning: Mary went and told Jesus' friends, who were mourning and weeping. Their tears showed how much they loved Him. No better news could reach sad disciples than that Christ is risen. We too can comfort hurting believers by sharing what we have seen of Christ.

The disciples did not believe Mary. They should have remembered that Jesus had told them this would happen. Yet their slowness helps us. Because they were hard to convince, we can trust them more when they later risked their lives to preach it.

Jesus then appeared to two followers walking into the country. This is the walk to Emmaus that Luke tells in full. He came "in a different form," meaning they did not know Him at first. Luke says their eyes were kept from seeing who He was.

The two went back and told the others, but they were not fully believed either. God wisely let the proof come step by step. That way the apostles' later certainty would rest on solid ground, not on quick belief.

Jesus appeared to the eleven apostles while they were at a meal. He scolded them for their unbelief and their stubborn, dull hearts. The problem was not weak evidence but hard hearts. We cannot excuse ourselves by saying we never saw Him, because we should trust those who did.

Jesus sends them into all the world to preach the gospel, which means the good news about Him. "Every creature" means every person, Jews and non-Jews alike. The eleven could not go everywhere, so they were to send others too. The command reaches gospel workers in every age.

Whoever truly believes in Christ will be saved, and baptism is the outward sign of that inner faith. Notice that Jesus says only unbelief brings condemnation, not a lack of baptism. Still, baptism is His command, and it should not be ignored. Those who reject the gospel have no other way to be saved.

Jesus promises signs to back up the gospel: driving out demons, speaking new languages, safety from snakes and poison, and healing the sick. We see these in Acts, like the tongues at Pentecost and Paul shaking off a viper. Not every believer would do these things, but some would, for the good of the whole church. The promise about poison is not a call to test God; it covers harm by accident or by enemies.

differ.view: These miracles were most likely given for a time, to support the gospel while it was new, and believers today should not expect them.
Every believer's faith still holds a hidden miraculous power, though it is often not used because of little faith; Wesley tells of a sudden healing during a sermon on this text.

notes.meaning: After speaking with them, Jesus was taken up into heaven. Luke and Acts tell more about this. To sit at God's right hand does not mean God has hands. It means Jesus holds the highest honor and power, resting from His finished work and ruling for the good of believers.

The once-frightened disciples went out and preached everywhere. The Lord worked with them and backed up their message with signs. The message came first, and the signs followed. Changed lives were also proof that the gospel is God's power, and the book of Acts tells the rest of the story.
